In the latest trading session, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) closed at $594.24, marking a -2.28% move from the previous day. The stock trailed the S&P 500, which registered a daily loss of 0.06%. Elsewhere, the Dow gained 0.38%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq lost 0.44%.

Shares of the chipmaker have appreciated by 17.82% over the course of the past month, outperforming the Computer and Technology sector's gain of 4.85%, and the S&P 500's gain of 2.36%.

Investors will be eagerly watching for the performance of Advanced Micro Devices in its upcoming earnings disclosure. The company's earnings report is set to be unveiled on November 3, 2026. It is anticipated that the company will report an EPS of $1.92, marking a 60% rise compared to the same quarter of the previous year. Alongside, our most recent consensus estimate is anticipating revenue of $13.07 billion, indicating a 41.34% upward movement from the same quarter last year.

For the full year, the Zacks Consensus Estimates project earnings of $7.5 per share and a revenue of $50.48 billion, demonstrating changes of +79.86% and +45.72%, respectively, from the preceding year.

Additionally, investors should keep an eye on any recent revisions to analyst forecasts for Advanced Micro Devices. These recent revisions tend to reflect the evolving nature of short-term business trends. As a result, upbeat changes in estimates indicate analysts' favorable outlook on the business health and profitability.

Our research shows that these estimate changes are directly correlated with near-term stock prices. To utilize this, we have created the Zacks Rank, a proprietary model that integrates these estimate changes and provides a functional rating system.

The Zacks Rank system, spanning from #1 (Strong Buy) to #5 (Strong Sell), boasts an impressive track record of outperformance, audited externally, with #1 ranked stocks yielding an average annual return of +25% since 1988. Over the past month, the Zacks Consensus EPS estimate has moved 0.06% higher. Advanced Micro Devices presently features a Zacks Rank of #3 (Hold).

Looking at valuation, Advanced Micro Devices is presently trading at a Forward P/E ratio of 81.07. Its industry sports an average Forward P/E of 20.49, so one might conclude that Advanced Micro Devices is trading at a premium comparatively.

One should further note that AMD currently holds a PEG ratio of 5.4. The PEG ratio bears resemblance to the frequently used P/E ratio, but this parameter also includes the company's expected earnings growth trajectory. As the market closed yesterday, the Computer - Integrated Systems industry was having an average PEG ratio of 0.57.

title: What Changed In Qualcomm's Story?
detail:
What Changed In Qualcomm's Story?
Trefis Team
Mon, October 12, 2026 at 2:55 PM PDT 4 min read
QCOM
^GSPC
AVGO
NVDA
INTC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Qualcomm (QCOM) stock is currently priced at 20.0 times earnings, trading below the 21.9 multiple of the S&P 500. Investors paying that price need a clear understanding of what they are buying, particularly as the company shifts its public priorities. Back in July 2025, executives anchored their presentations on sales targets for automotive and IoT chips, which power connected consumer and industrial devices. By the latest call, those figures had taken a back seat. So what does Qualcomm lead with now?

Qualcomm Is Entering A New Chip Market

Executives are now highlighting chips for data centers, a market the company is only just entering. During the fiscal Q3 2026 earnings call in July 2026, management stated that Qualcomm was "expanding into the data center with 4 unique product lines."

That represents a distinct shift in messaging. During the fiscal Q3 2025 call a year earlier, leadership instead focused on a fiscal 2029 target of $22 billion in combined automotive and IoT revenue.

Those alternative revenue streams remain critical because Qualcomm relies heavily on smartphones. Its chip business made up 87% of revenue in fiscal 2025, and phones generated $5.1 billion of that segment's $8.5 billion in revenue during fiscal Q3 2026. And on its July 2026 call, Qualcomm said it expected its share of the then-upcoming iPhone launch to be materially lower than its prior estimate of 20%. Management characterizes this push beyond phones as its diversification strategy.

How Big Are Qualcomm's Old And New Priorities?

Qualcomm already reports its automotive and IoT results, whereas the data center business remains mostly a forecast. The company posted automotive revenue of $1.6 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, marking a 61% increase from a year earlier. In the same period, IoT revenue grew 9% to $1.8 billion.

The data center operation is still in its earliest stages. Wafer production has begun on Qualcomm's two custom data center chip wins, and these components are due to start generating revenue in the December quarter. Looking further out, management forecast data center revenue of $5 billion in fiscal 2027.

Automotive and IoT products still represent the larger piece of management's long-term plan. Executives now expect to generate more than $24 billion from cars and IoT in fiscal 2029, compared to more than $15 billion from data centers. The total fiscal 2029 outlook for sales outside phones currently stands at $40 billion.

Can Qualcomm Investors Take Comfort In This?

For the automotive and IoT segments, the internal projections offer reassurance. Management maintained and even expanded its prior targets: the car and IoT portion of the fiscal 2029 outlook is now larger than the forecast provided in July 2025. The company also guided for another record automotive performance in fiscal Q4 2026, projecting revenue growth of approximately 60% from a year earlier.

title: Nvidia and AMD Reached a Historic Valuation Split. 1 Stock Is Far Safer.
detail:
Nvidia and AMD Reached a Historic Valuation Split. 1 Stock Is Far Safer.
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Mon, October 12, 2026 at 12:50 PM PDT 4 min read
NVDA
AMD
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) are similar companies. While AMD's consumer business is larger and it has a wider product lineup, these two compete head-to-head in arguably the most important technological battle in the world: GPUs for artificial intelligence computing. While Nvidia stormed out to an early lead at the start of the AI boom in 2023, AMD has clawed its way back and is offering viable products that could serve as an alternative to Nvidia's product lineup.

If you ask the market, AMD is clearly winning the battle and stealing market share, which is why its stock has nearly tripled in 2026, compared with Nvidia's 23% gain. But this mismatch in stock performance has caused the two stocks' valuations to uncouple.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

This could be a huge warning flag for one (or both) of the stocks, and investors must understand what's going on and take proper action.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
AMD's valuation has gotten out of control

Over the past few years, Nvidia and AMD's valuations have been fairly in line with each other, outside of the last six months.

AMD PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts

Since the end of spring, AMD's stock has been on an absolute tear, reaching heights never seen before. It now has a market cap of about $1 trillion, but does it actually deserve it? The question of what a fair price is for AMD's stock is tricky. AMD is doing its best since the AI boom kicked off in 2023.

AMD Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts

Its profit margins are at recent highs, and its growth rate is reaching new levels. That has caused the market to reprice AMD's stock, as it deserved, but the level it has reached seems a bit extreme. Although AMD is doing the best it's ever done, it's still nowhere near where Nvidia is now. And that's the major problem with AMD's stock.

AMD isn't priced correctly

During Nvidia's last quarter, it grew revenue at a 106% pace and reached a projected margin of 62%. That makes it a far stronger company than AMD, and from that information alone, there's no reason to bet on AMD over Nvidia.

Next year, AMD is expected to close the gap, but not by a huge margin. The average Wall Street analyst expects Nvidia revenue to grow at a 68% pace to $692 billion next year. AMD's revenue growth is expected to be about 75%, reaching $89 billion. So, AMD is expected to overtake Nvidia's growth rate, but with the two only a few percentage points apart, that's really not much of a separation.

title: What Does NVIDIA Offer That Marvell Does Not?
detail:
What Does NVIDIA Offer That Marvell Does Not?
Trefis Team

NVDA
AVGO
AMD
INTC

Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Investors buy Marvell Technology (MRVL) and NVIDIA (NVDA) to capture spending on artificial intelligence data centers, but the two companies generate revenue differently. NVIDIA sells the full AI system, while Marvell supplies custom chips for individual cloud customers and the components that connect chips inside a data center. Marvell has been the much stronger stock. It returned 222% over the past twelve months, compared with 25% for NVIDIA. What has each company told investors to expect from here?

What Marvell And NVIDIA Have Said Since August

Marvell recently raised its financial outlook, although NVIDIA still anticipates a faster pace of growth. On August 27, Marvell increased its fiscal 2027 revenue outlook to roughly $12 billion and lifted its fiscal 2028 outlook to about $18 billion, up from $16.5 billion a quarter earlier. This new outlook means revenue growth of about 50% in fiscal 2028, and it includes the custom business more than doubling.

Then, on October 6, Marvell raised its fiscal 2028 outlook again, to about $20 billion, and forecast fiscal 2031 revenue of $70 billion to $90 billion during its Investor Day. For context, the company generated $9.5 billion in revenue over the past twelve months.

NVIDIA delivered a different kind of update on August 26. Management provided a forecast a year ahead for the first time, projecting revenue growth of about 70% in fiscal 2028, though they noted supply constraints would hold that figure back. NVIDIA had no earlier forecast to raise. During the same call, the company said rising memory costs would pull its gross margin from 75% to a low of 71% to 72% in the fourth quarter.

What Do Marvell And NVIDIA Give Up For Sales?

Both companies expect lower gross margins in the coming quarters. Marvell guided its fiscal Q3 2027 gross margin to between 57.5% and 58.5%, down from the 58.9% it reported for Q2, both on a non-GAAP basis. Management said the main reason is the custom business, which is ramping up quickly.

Even so, Marvell expects its profit to grow faster than its sales. On the August call, the finance chief said non-GAAP operating margin was likely to enter Marvell's 38% to 40% long-term target range in fiscal Q4 2027.

NVIDIA posted a gross margin of 75% in fiscal Q2 2027, and management expects it to bottom at 71% to 72% in Q4. The chip maker is also using its own balance sheet to back its customers. It has invested nearly $50 billion in frontier AI labs. Management expects AI labs to make up roughly a quarter of its business in the year ahead.
